title: React Router v6
subtitle: Client-side routing — Route, Link, useNavigate, useParams, and nested routes
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: React SPAs render everything client-side, but users expect URL-based navigation — back/forward buttons, shareable links, bookmarks. Without a router, the URL doesn't change when you navigate between sections.
whyItExists.solution: React Router v6 is the standard routing library. It maps URL patterns to components and provides hooks for navigation. The browser's History API updates the URL without a full page load.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any multi-page React app — dashboards, e-commerce, documentation sites, social apps.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Single-page apps with no navigation (a widget, a modal, a single screen). For frameworks like Next.js or Remix, use their built-in routing instead of React Router.

explainModes.beginner: React Router lets you show different components for different URLs — like tabs but the URL changes too. Wrap your app in <BrowserRouter>. Use <Route path='/about' element={<About />} /> to map a URL to a component. Use <Link to='/about'> instead of <a href='/about'> to navigate without a page reload.
explainModes.simple: Setup: <BrowserRouter><Routes><Route path='/' element={<Home />} /><Route path='/about' element={<About />} /></Routes></BrowserRouter>. Navigation: <Link to='/about'>. Programmatic: const nav = useNavigate(); nav('/dashboard'). URL params: <Route path='/users/:id' /> → const { id } = useParams(). Nested routes: <Route path='/dashboard' element={<Dashboard />}><Route index element={<Overview />} /><Route path='stats' element={<Stats />} /></Route> — Dashboard renders <Outlet /> where children appear.
explainModes.standard: Route matching: v6 uses relative paths and is smarter — no need for exact prop. Index routes: the default child route. Outlet: renders the matched child route inside a parent layout. Layout routes: a Route with element={<Layout />} but no path — wraps children in the layout. useNavigate options: nav(-1) goes back, nav('/path', { replace: true }) replaces history (no back button). NavLink: like Link but adds an active class when the route matches.
explainModes.technical: BrowserRouter vs HashRouter: BrowserRouter uses HTML5 History API (clean URLs: /about). HashRouter uses URL hash (#/about) — works without server configuration. For a SPA deployed on GitHub Pages, use HashRouter or configure the server to serve index.html for all paths. useLocation: returns the current location object ({ pathname, search, hash, state }). useSearchParams: reads and sets URL query string params (?q=react). Lazy loading routes: React.lazy + Suspense defer loading route components until they're navigated to — reduces initial bundle size.
explainModes.deepDive: React Router v6 architecture: Routes component uses a Fibonacci score to rank matching routes — more specific paths score higher. * catches all unmatched paths (404 page). Data loading: React Router v6.4+ (with createBrowserRouter instead of BrowserRouter) adds data loading with loader functions — each route can define a loader that fetches data before rendering the component. This is the same pattern used in Remix (React Router's framework mode). Nested layouts: deeply nested routes share ancestor layouts — each level of nesting adds a parent layout component that renders its children via Outlet. This is how most dashboards are structured: a root layout with Navbar, a section layout with Sidebar, and individual page components.

questions.question: What is the difference between `<Link to='/about'>` and `<a href='/about'>`?
options: There is no difference — they work the same way in React
Link navigates client-side (no page reload, no new HTTP request); a tag causes a full page reload, losing all React state
Link only works inside a BrowserRouter; a tag works everywhere
a tag is faster because it uses the browser's native navigation
questions.explanation: React Router's <Link> uses the History API to update the URL and re-render the matched components — no HTTP request, no page reload, React state is preserved. A plain <a href> triggers a full page reload: all React state is lost, the app re-initializes from scratch, and a network request is made. Always use Link (or NavLink for active-class support) for internal navigation in a React Router app.

faq.q: When do I use useNavigate vs Link?
faq.a: Use Link (or NavLink) for clickable navigation elements in JSX — menus, buttons, text links. Use useNavigate for programmatic navigation triggered by events — after a form submits successfully, after an async operation completes, or when a condition is met. useNavigate gives you the navigate function: call navigate('/dashboard') or navigate(-1) to go back.

examples: navigate('/login', { state: { from: location.pathname } }) — redirect with return URL
